title: Proteomic and Genomic Discovery of Targets for Atrial Cardiopathy-Related Cardiovascular Outcomes
text:
Atrial cardiopathy is now recognized as an important risk factor for many cardiovascular complications
attributed to atrial fibrillation. The goal of this project is to use proteomics and genomics to discover new
molecular targets for treatments preventing cardiovascular complications related to atrial cardiopathy.

title: Bhlhe40 Regulation of T Cell Function During Cancer Immunotherapy
text:
T cells are specialized white blood cells that can recognize and destroy tumors in response to cancer
immunotherapy treatments. We recently found that a protein called Bhlhe40 is required by T cells for tumor
regression in response to immune checkpoint immunotherapy and our goal is to understand how Bhlhe40
regulates T cells to enable them to eliminate tumors under certain conditions. We anticipate this work will provide
insights that will lead to development of improved cancer immunotherapies that are needed, as many cancer
patients do not experience clinical benefit from current immunotherapy treatments.

title: Physical resilience is a predictor of healthy aging
text:
The overall goal of this proposal is to obtain a better mechanistic understanding of resilience
to aging at the molecular, cellular, organ, and systemic physiological levels in order to identify
therapeutic targets. The public health significance relates to the ability to therapeutically
enhance resilience to aging and age-related diseases in individuals predicted to be less
resilient.

title: Harvard/Stanford GTN Program:  Novel targeted therapeutics for glioblastoma
text:
(three sentences)
Tumors of the brain are the most common cause of cancer-related death in children, the third leading cause
of cancer-related death among middle aged men and the fourth leading cause of death for women
between15-34 years of age. The most common (in children) and the most lethal (in young adults)
form of brain cancer is the cohort of tumors called “glioma”. This goal of this Specialized Program of
Research Excellence (“SPORE”) initiative is to develop non-toxic, “precision medicines” for gliomas of
children and young adults.

title: Water for Health: Strengthening Tribal Action for Cancer Prevention
text: For decades, the Strong Heart Study (SHS) has collaborated with several Tribal Nations and their citizens in the Northern Plains, Southern Plains, and Southwest to improve cardiovascular health through various multi-level interventions and state-of-the-art epidemiologic research. Tribal communities often experience significantly elevated drinking water arsenic and uranium exposures in both private wells and regulated public drinking water systems. However, the contribution of these modifiable drinking water exposures in arsenic and uranium-associated cancer incidence mortality remains poorly characterized. Arsenic- and uranium- associated cancers are of increasing concern for SHS and other Tribal communities nationwide, as many experience high incidence rates for these cancers (lung, bladder, kidney, pancreas, prostate). The objective of the proposed project is to support multi-level interventions to reduce water arsenic and uranium for Tribal communities, with the ultimate goal of reducing arsenic and uranium associated cancers. The proposed project is grounded in a conceptual model linking local social-ecological frameworks for health outcomes and differences in water arsenic exposures with frameworks that weave mainstream science with community knowledge. In Aim 1, we will comprehensively characterize exposure to arsenic and uranium in unregulated well and public water systems across all SHS communities and disseminate individualized dashboards to their Tribal Nations. In addition to leveraging available resources that have not been compiled for stakeholder use, we will extend process-based models for estimating groundwater arsenic and geospatial models of arsenic/uranium in public water to all SHS communities. In Aim 2, we will conduct state-of-the-art epidemiologic analyses to evaluate the association between water arsenic and uranium with incident and fatal cancers of the lung, bladder, kidney, pancreas, and prostate in the SHS cohorts, with a focus on estimating the impacts of potential interventions on cancer rates. These data are critical because Tribal populations remain unrepresented in the epidemiologic science that drives drinking water standards. In Aim 3, we will conduct formative research with the SHS communities and comprehensively review successful multi-level intervention plans with community priorities, needs, strengths, and challenges, with the ultimate goal of supporting communities to develop culturally relevant and individualized intervention plans to reduce water arsenic and uranium. Our proposal brings together a multi-disciplinary, multi-site team, and leverages decades of collaboration and community engagement with SHS communities across all three SHS study sites. The proposed study responds directly to the NIMHD-identified need for community-driven prevention strategies to reduce the impact of arsenic and uranium-associated cancers for Tribal Nations and their members.

title: Novel MRI Approaches to Improve Presurgical Benefit-Risk Evaluation in Pediatric Epilepsy Surgery
text:
This renewal application will investigate a novel deep learning-based preoperative benefit-risk analysis tools for
pediatric drug-resistant focal epilepsy that can precisely optimize the spatial converage of intracranial EEG to
localize all plausible epileptogenic zone (EZ) sites in non-lesional epilepsy patients using clinical MRI data,
accurately provide an optimal resection boundary of the EZ resulting in the maximized benefit (seizure freedom)
and minimized risk (functional deficit including motor, language, hearing, and vision), and objectively quantify
the degree of epilepsy svereity underlying a high likelihood of neurocognitive decline. The results of this
application will significantly reduce failed seizure control, postsurgical functional complications, and the risk of
severe cognitive impairment in pediatric drug-resistant epilepsy surgery. Thus, it is anticipated that the
develpted tools can support earlier surgical decision-making by families and clinical providers to enhance
postoperative outcomes.

title: Improving the Detection and Understanding of Aortic Aneurysms through Large-Scale Radiologic and Genetic Risk Assessments
text:
Early detection and better understanding of aortic aneurysms can improve clinical care and save lives. By
applying a robust automated analysis to routine medical imaging, we can find aneurysms missed by current
screening practices and learn how they develop over time. Linking these findings with clinical and genetic
factors will improve our ability to monitor aneurysm growth, understand its mechanisms, and ultimately
enhance patient outcomes.

title: Function of the METTL3-NUP93 complex-mediated nuclear export of m6A-modified mRNAs in castration-resistant prostate cancer.
text:
Nuclear pore complex (NPC)-associated cofactors are shown to cooperate with the regulators of N6-
adenosine methylation (m6A) to control the nuclear export of mRNAs, which is essential for normal functions of
certain physiological processes. However, no studies have ever investigated the role of this cooperation in
cancer. Our preliminary data demonstrated that the m6A methyltransferase METTL3 directly binds to a
component of NPCs called NUP93 in cancer cells, which ensures the efficient export of m6A-containing
mRNAs. Interestingly, a subgroup of the mRNA cargos of the METTL3-NUP93 complex in prostate cancer
(PCa) cells are functionally enriched in biosynthesis of androgen, the ligand for the main driver of PCa
progression — androgen receptor (AR). Thus, in this study we aim to (1). Elucidate how the METTL3-NUP93
complex selects the target mRNAs and facilitates their nuclear export; (2). Investigate how the m6A-METTL3-
NUP93 axis increases the intratumoral androgen levels and stimulates AR activity; and (3). Evaluate the
therapeutic potential of targeting the m6A-METTL3-NUP93 axis for the treatment of castration-resistant
prostate cancer (CRPC), the most aggressive form of the disease. As such, our research will furnish novel
insights into the functions of m6A and NPCs in PCa progression and offer promising anticancer drug targets.

title: Behavioral and neural mechanisms mediating social motivation in a rat model for ASD
text:
Autism spectrum disorder is characterized by impairments in the motivation to engage in social
interactions. By using novel computational tracking system with a novel rodent model of social self-
administration in rats with a mutation in the Shank3 gene (a rat model for ASD), in combination with cutting-
edge tools and circuitry manipulation approaches, this proposal will determine the behavioral and neural
mechanisms mediating the autism-like-induced shift in social motivation. This research will provide
collaborative potential and introduce new ideas and a new conceptual framework to ASD research.

title: Perisomatic inhibition in epilepsy
text: Inhibitory neurotransmission controls the activity and synchrony of excitatory neurons, and impaired inhibition contributes to the pathomechanism of neurological disorders such as epilepsy. The current experiments will determine whether specific types of inhibitory neurons are more effective at suppressing epileptic activity in the neuronal circuit without disrupting information encoding and may identify strategies to prevent seizures without adverse effects on cognitive function.

title: MHC GENETIC TYPING CORE
text: To enhance the Johns Hopkins University pigtail macaque colony as a research resource for studying multiple facets of HIV infection, we have concentrated on improving our understanding of pigtail macaque (Macaca nemestrina) genetics. We continue to identify and study pigtail macaque MHC class I and MHC class II alleles using state of the art sequencing approaches working in collaboration with Dr. David O’Connor at the University of Wisconsin. This ongoing effort has discovered novel MHC alleles and defined MHC class I haplotypes in pigtail macaques. To broaden the scope of our efforts beyond MHC, we have worked with Dr. Michael Snyder’s team at Stanford to generate a de novo assembly of the pigtail macaque genome that used long-read sequencing technology. This pigtail macaque resource will facilitate use of functional genomics approaches in SIV studies. Expanding the genetic data available for pigtail macaques will a) increase the research utility of pigtail macaques and b) assist in genetic management of the JHU colony with guidance from Dr. Sree Kanthaswamy, a long term collaborator. Specific Aim 4 is to continue to characterize pigtail macaque MHC class I and MHC class II genotypes in JHU colony-born animals using state of the art deep sequencing approaches, thereby enhancing genetic management of the breeding colony rigor and promoting reproducibility of SIV/macaque models of HIV.

title: CORE 2: Genetic Engineering Core
text: Genome engineering technologies permit the alteration of DNA sequences or changes in gene expression, enabling the creation of modified models to test biological hypotheses in living cells and organisms. The mission of our Genetic Engineering (GE) Core is to design and optimize genome and epigenome editing strategies to help define the relationships between hematopoiesis and the progression of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), which remain a leading cause of death. Our wider Program Project will bring together field-leading researchers to close this gap in knowledge by elucidating and investigating factors that connect hematopoiesis and CVD. Thus, there is tremendous opportunity to address these outstanding questions by leveraging leading-edge technologies like genome and epigenome editing tools to engineer hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in vitro or to create new mouse models to investigate CVD. The GE Core will play a collaborative dual role in this consortium. First, the primary function of our Core is to serve the Projects using pre-existing GE tools by designing, optimizing, and implementing a variety of editing approaches for use in HSPCs (prior to transplant into live recipient mice) or to create novel animal models, both of which will expedite our PPG objectives. We will implement streamlined in silico and experimental methods to design and validate GE strategies to test hypotheses from all Project teams, will optimize gene editing strategies to knockout genes in cells or construct new animal models (Projects 2-4), will deploy epigenetic methods to alter gene expression (Project 1), and will assist with the design and validation of CRISPR screens (Project 4). Our GE Core will implement various GE technologies capable of a diversity of edit types (e.g. nuclease, base editors, prime editing, or sequence insertion methods) to perturb or install candidate genes nominated by Projects 1-4. The second mission of our Core is to develop next-generation technologies that overcome key issues of CRISPR-based GE methods, further enabling our key experimental goals. To do so, we will utilize a suite of protein engineering methods to develop novel CRISPR-Cas editors with improved properties (e.g. enzymes with enhanced on-target efficiency), with expanded scopes of edit outcomes and edit sizes (e.g. large insertions), all while maintaining stringent genome-wide safety in HSPCs and other primary cell types. Our collaborative efforts with the Projects will place an emphasis on innovation to expedite the key objectives of this Program. The Projects will have immediate access to the most advanced state-of-the-art editing technologies and methods, which together will enable rapid, efficient, and safe genetic edits to investigate the connections between hematopoiesis and CVD. More broadly, these advances will be applicable to the study of cardiovascular and hematopoietic disorders, with a path to new therapeutics.

title: Structural Biology of Alpha-Synuclein in Lewy Body Dementia
text:
This project will improve understanding of disease mechanisms in Lewy Body Dementia. In addition, improved
understanding of alpha-synuclein fibril structure will promote the development of biomarkers and treatments for
Lewy Body Dementia.

title: Statistical software for analyzing genomics data
text:
We are developing statistical methods to help scientists tackle a diverse range of problems: understanding the
effects of genetic variation on fundamental biological processes; identifying sets of related genes that explain the
results of an experiment; and discovering relationships among samples (e.g., cells, genes, people), for example to
identify cell or disease subtypes. The focus of the proposed project is to make these statistical methods available
to the research community as high-quality statistical software. These methods and software have the potential to
help us better understand the biology of disease, leading eventually to new therapies or treatments.

title: NeuroData AI Summer School: Advanced Training in Neurophysiology Data Analysis
text:
The NeuroData AI Summer School will train 35 researchers annually in AI-enhanced neurophysiology data
analysis through an intensive five-day residential program that addresses the critical skills gap preventing
effective utilization of the 380+ open datasets (350+ TB) available through DANDI and major collaborative
efforts like the International Brain Laboratory and Allen Institute's OpenScope. Building upon four years of
successful NeuroDataReHack programs (unanimous 5/5 satisfaction ratings), participants will receive
hands-on training in standardized data formats (NWB, DANDI), state-of-the-art analysis tools (SpikeInterface,
Pynapple, VAME), and cutting-edge AI applications including foundation models and machine learning
approaches, while conducting collaborative research projects using real datasets from OpenScope, IBL, and
MICrONS. This nationally organized program will create a cadre of researchers skilled in modern
computational approaches to neurophysiology while establishing sustainable educational infrastructure through
publicly available materials and fostering a community of practice that catalyzes the cultural shift toward
collaborative, reproducible neuroscience research.

title: Cancer Genomics Facility
text: Cancer Genomics Facility (CGF) Cancer genomic and transcriptomic studies have grown increasingly more complex with a wide variety of techniques now available, including whole exome, genome and transcriptome; methylation; single cell sequencing; etc. For both new and established investigators this landscape can be difficult to navigate. The Cancer Genomics Facility (CGF) is a resource that is intimately tied to the Cancer Bioinformatics Services (CBS) and Biostatistics Facility (BF), providing a seamless concierge service for HCC investigators navigating this complex landscape. The CGF offers next generation sequencing support for clinical, translational and discovery-based cancer biology with a scope of other services that span from customized arrays to single cell genomics. Implementation of high throughput sequencing approaches continues to require expensive instrumentation; capabilities that lie beyond the scope of most individual laboratories. The CGF allows for these investigators to gain access to state-of-the-art next-generation sequencing at reduced rates. These services paired with informatics and statistical support by CBS and BF allows for investigators to explore all aspects of cancer genomics.

title: Identifying mechanisms ofsynapse maturation at neuronal subtype resolution
text:
Our brain function relies on the formation and maintenance of precise neural circuits among various subtypes of
neurons, whose disruption contributes to many mental disorders including autism spectrum disorder. Neural
circuits are mediated by synapses with distinct characteristics between neuronal subtypes and across
developmental stages. Characterizing the diversity of synapses and elucidating the underlying developmental
mechanisms will offer perspectives into how circuit specificity is established and how it goes awry in mental
disorders.

title: Cardiogenesis: Molecular Mechanisms
text:
Valvuloseptal defects account for the majority of congenital heart defects, which are the most common human
birth defect. Down Syndrome, involving trisomy of chromosome 21 affects 1 in 700 live births and causes
valvuloseptal heart defects. We will investigate the molecular mechanisms that cause valvuloseptal defects in
mouse and human models, including models of Down Syndrome, to understand the sets of genes that when
improperly regulated cause syndromic and non-syndromic heart defects.

title: Mapping the blood cancer exposome for environmental risk profiles of mature B-cell neoplasms
text:
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma and multiple myeloma are the most commonly diagnosed mature B-cell neoplasms in
the world. Disease risk is driven by a combination of environmental and genetic factors, with environment
being largely unstudied and unknown. We will apply exposomic methods in a nested case–control study to
measure thousands of environmental chemicals and endogenous metabolites present before diagnosis to
identify patterns of chemical exposures predicting future risk of disease and discover key insights into
mechanisms underlying mature B-cell neoplasm pathogenesis—both of which are needed to improve
outcomes from these cancers.

title: Using complex video stimuli to elucidate atypical brain functioning in ASD
text:
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects approximately 1% of the
population, yet its neural and cognitive bases remain elusive. This proposal will use complex video stimuli
together with functional neuroimaging (fMRI) and computational methods to identify brain regions that best
predict ASD groups, subgroups, and traits, identify the underlying stimulus features that drive these neural
differences, and make the data and tools we generate maximally available for others to use and build upon.
